# War Scroll (Milhamah) — Reader's Guide

---

## At a Glance

| | |
|---|---|
| **Attribution** | Anonymous; likely composed by a priestly author with access to military terminology and Temple liturgical traditions |
| **Actual Composition** | Core material possibly late 2nd century BCE; final form c. 50–25 BCE; our manuscript (1QM) copied c. 1st century BCE |
| **Language** | Hebrew (elevated, archaic prose with liturgical passages in heightened poetic register) |
| **Audience** | Community members awaiting the final eschatological war; leaders who would direct the military and liturgical operations of that war |
| **Genre** | Eschatological battle plan / liturgical warfare manual / apocalyptic vision |
| **Length** | 19 columns; substantially complete though some columns are fragmentary; supplemented by multiple fragmentary copies from Cave 4 (4QM fragments) |
| **In One Sentence** | The War Scroll describes the final forty-year cosmic war between the Sons of Light and the Sons of Darkness in meticulous military and liturgical detail — a war that is simultaneously a human campaign and an angelic battle, simultaneously historical and eschatological, in which Israel's victory is certain because God himself has decreed it from before the foundation of the world. |

---

## Sections Overview

**Column 1: The Opening Battle Order**
The scroll opens in medias res with a statement of the conflict: the Sons of Light, led by the tribe of Levi, Judah, and Benjamin, will go to war against the Sons of Darkness — specifically the Kittim of Assyria and the "violators of the covenant," meaning apostate Jews. The Kittim is a code word the Qumran community used for the dominant imperial power of their day; in the earliest uses (cf. Numbers 24:24, Daniel 11:30) it referred to sea-peoples from the west, but by the first century BCE in Qumran texts it clearly designates Rome. Column 1 also lays out the forty-year structure of the war: the first years against specific enemies, then engagement with the nations of the earth in order, a sabbatical year of rest, until the final victory.

**Columns 2–9: Military Organization and Equipment**
These columns constitute the manual proper: the organization of infantry and cavalry units; the exact dimensions and inscriptions of the trumpets used for signaling (no fewer than six different trumpet calls are described, each for a specific military maneuver); the dimensions and inscriptions of the banners carried by each unit; the weapons and armor of the foot soldiers; the formations for engagement — including a three-line battle array and flanking maneuvers. The level of detail is extraordinary. The banner inscriptions are particularly striking: each banner proclaims a divine title or a theological affirmation about the war's purpose.

**Columns 10–12: Liturgical Elements — Prayers and Blessings**
The war is not only a military operation. Before and after each engagement, priests lead the community in prayer. Column 10 contains an extended praise of God as the warrior-king of Israel, drawing heavily on the Psalms and on Moses's Song of the Sea (Exodus 15). Column 11 contains a meditation on the mystery of divine warfare — God has revealed his power to the angels, and now that power is extended to the human army. Column 12 describes blessings for victory and thanksgiving after battle. These liturgical sections are among the most elevated Hebrew prose in the Dead Sea Scrolls.

**Columns 13–14: The High Priest's Speech and the Role of Angels**
The high priest addresses the army before the climactic battle. He invokes the precedent of Goliath's defeat by David — a single divine champion defeating an overwhelming enemy through God's power rather than human strength. Column 13 also contains a hymn that explicitly names the archangel Michael as the leader of the angelic army fighting alongside the Sons of Light. This is the clearest statement in the scroll of the supernatural dimension of the war: human soldiers fight alongside angelic warriors, and the battle is won not by human strategy but by divine decree.

**Columns 15–19: The Final Engagement**
The concluding columns describe the final great battle in three engagements, each of which the Sons of Darkness initially seem to win, before God intervenes and the Sons of Light prevail on the third assault. This three-part structure may reflect a liturgical or dramatic pattern. Column 19 (partially damaged) apparently concludes with hymns of thanksgiving, including a passage praising God for his ultimate defeat of the forces of evil. The Kittim — Rome — are defeated. The age of wickedness ends. The age of God's direct rule begins.

---

## The World Behind the Text

The War Scroll was written by people who expected to fight a real war. This must be held clearly in view. Modern readers are sometimes tempted to read it as purely symbolic or literary — an elaborate metaphor for spiritual combat. The Qumran community believed that the cosmic conflict between good and evil they experienced spiritually, the historical conflict with Rome they experienced politically, and the eschatological war they found prophesied in Daniel and elsewhere were not three different things but three dimensions of a single reality that was approaching its final resolution.

The Maccabean revolt (168–164 BCE) had demonstrated to a generation of Jews that a small force of faithful men, fighting under God's banner, could defeat a vastly superior imperial army. The Maccabees had rededicated the Temple. But the subsequent Hasmonean dynasty had become corrupt, had illegitimately seized the high priesthood, and had eventually invited Roman intervention (63 BCE, when Pompey walked into the Holy of Holies). For the Qumran community, this trajectory confirmed that the Maccabean victory had not been the final eschatological war but only a preview. The real war was still coming.

The military detail in the scroll draws on multiple sources: the holy war tradition in Deuteronomy and Joshua (the camp must be ritually pure; God is the actual warrior; Israel's role is faithful obedience); the battles described in the books of Maccabees; possibly direct observation of Roman military formations, since several tactical features described in the War Scroll correspond to Roman legionary tactics of the late Republic. The community may have studied their enemies carefully in order to defeat them.

Purity was central to the war camp. The scroll explicitly bars from the battle any man who was ritually impure, any man with physical defects, any man who had experienced a nocturnal emission — because the holy angels are present in the camp, and their presence requires the same level of purity as the Temple sanctuary. The war camp is a mobile Temple. This explains a feature that otherwise seems merely obsessive: the extraordinary attention to purity and physical perfection among the combatants is theologically driven, not a matter of military fitness.

The scroll also reflects a world in which Israel's humiliation under Gentile domination was felt as a theological crisis. The nations of the earth had dominated Israel for centuries. The Persian empire, the Ptolemies, the Seleucids, and now Rome — one foreign power after another had ruled over the people of the covenant. The War Scroll answers this by asserting that this domination is temporary, by divine decree, and that its time is almost up. God has appointed the dominion of Belial for this era; he will end it. The certainty of victory is not wishful thinking but theological claim.

---

## Why This Text Was Written

The War Scroll served several overlapping functions.

At its most practical level, it is a preparation text. The community expected the war to come within their lifetime or within a few generations. They were actively preparing for it. This scroll told them how. The military details — trumpet signals, battle formations, banner inscriptions — were not academic exercises but operational planning for a war they intended to fight.

But the scroll also served a consolation and formation function. Living under Roman rule in the Judean wilderness, cut off from the Temple, looked down on by the Jerusalem establishment — the Yahad needed to maintain the conviction that their suffering was purposeful and temporary. The War Scroll provided that conviction in the most dramatic possible terms: the forces arrayed against them were not just the Romans but Belial himself and all his angels; and Belial would lose. This is the same function that the book of Revelation served for persecuted Christians under Roman rule: not a prediction of events to be decoded but a vision of ultimate reality that sustains resistance and hope.

The scroll also functioned as liturgical preparation. The prayers and hymns embedded in the military instructions were probably used in actual community worship. Reciting the hymn of column 10 in the context of community prayer was not merely academic — it was a practice of aligning the community's self-understanding with the cosmic drama they believed they inhabited.

Finally, the scroll served a theological clarifying function. Why do the wicked prosper? Why does Rome rule over God's people? Why does the Jerusalem establishment flourish while the righteous suffer in exile? The War Scroll's answer is: because God has appointed this era of Belial's dominion as a probationary time for his elect, and it will end when God acts. The scroll names the enemy, assigns him a theological status (subject to God, operating on divine permission, doomed), and places the community's suffering within a narrative of ultimate vindication.

---

## How to Read This Text

**Read column 1 as the interpretive key.** Before diving into the detailed military regulations, grasp the fundamental narrative: forty years, Israel and the angels against the Kittim and the nations, final victory, new age. The subsequent detail is in service of this narrative arc.

**Do not skip the banner and trumpet inscriptions.** They are the scroll's theology in compressed form. Each inscription is a mini-creed. The trumpet for "the call to battle" is inscribed "the called of God." The trumpet for "the slain" is inscribed "the hand of God in battle." These inscriptions tell you what the community believed they were doing in the war: not fighting for land or political independence but enacting the judgment of God.

**Read the liturgical sections (cols. 10–12) as actual prayers.** Imagine them spoken before an assembled community, at dawn, before a battle — the high priest's voice carrying over hundreds of armed men. The prayers are not decorative; they constitute the meaning of the military action.

**Compare the three-round battle structure (cols. 15–19) with Revelation 19–20.** In both texts, the final battle is not a single engagement but a sequence in which the forces of darkness seem initially to gain ground before God's decisive intervention. Both texts feature the appearance of heavenly armies fighting alongside the human faithful. The structural parallel suggests a shared apocalyptic template, probably rooted in the "Day of the LORD" tradition in the Prophets.

**Hold the text's certainty and its anguish together.** The scroll is absolutely certain of ultimate victory. But it was written by a community living in the wilderness, excluded from the Temple, politically powerless, waiting for a war that had not yet come. The certainty is not the certainty of the comfortable but the certainty of the desperate who have staked everything on a promise.

---

## The Threads

**Hebrew Bible**
- **Deuteronomy 20; 23:9–14**: The holy war regulations — the purity of the camp, the disqualifications from battle, God as the actual warrior — provide the War Scroll's foundational legal framework. The scroll expands these regulations enormously but the Deuteronomic logic is unchanged.
- **Numbers 10:1–10**: The use of trumpets for assembling the community and signaling military movements comes directly from Numbers. The War Scroll transforms this into an elaborate system of six or more distinct trumpet calls.
- **Exodus 15 (Song of the Sea)**: The great victory hymn after crossing the Red Sea — "The LORD is a warrior, the LORD is his name" — is the template for the War Scroll's liturgical sections. Column 10 is essentially a meditation on Exodus 15 expanded into the eschatological frame.
- **Daniel 10–12**: The most direct scriptural predecessor. Daniel's vision of the angelic prince Michael fighting on behalf of Israel against the angelic princes of Persia and Greece, the time of unprecedented tribulation, and the final resurrection — this is the War Scroll's apocalyptic framework in embryo.
- **Ezekiel 38–39 (Gog and Magog)**: The invasion of the nations against Israel, God's supernatural intervention with fire and plague, the great feast of judgment — Ezekiel's Gog oracle is a structural predecessor to the War Scroll's final battle sequence.
- **Isaiah 31:8; Micah 5**: Prophetic oracles of divine warrior victory against Assyria/the nations inform the scroll's confidence in God's direct military intervention.

**New Testament**
- **Revelation 12, 16, 19–20**: The structural parallels are remarkable: Michael and his angels at war with the dragon and his angels (Rev. 12, cf. 1QM 17); the final battle of God and the Lamb against the kings of the earth and their armies (Rev. 19, cf. 1QM 1, 15–19); the defeat of the Beast and False Prophet; the binding of Satan for a period, then final defeat. John of Patmos and the War Scroll author drew on the same Daniel-rooted apocalyptic tradition.
- **1 Thessalonians 5:8; Ephesians 6:10–17**: Paul's armor of God passage and his description of the believer's spiritual weapons are often read as pure metaphor, but they may draw on the same tradition of holy war spirituality that produced the War Scroll — adapted into the register of individual spiritual combat.
- **Luke 1:51–53 (Magnificat)**: Mary's song of the powerful brought low and the humble exalted echoes the War Scroll's theology of God vindicating the weak against the strong.
- **2 Corinthians 10:3–4**: "Though we walk in the flesh, we are not waging war according to the flesh. For the weapons of our warfare are not of the flesh but have divine power." Paul's adaptation of holy war imagery into spiritual terms suggests the tradition was alive and available for reinterpretation.

**Other Dead Sea Scrolls**
- **4QM (4Q491–496)**: Multiple fragmentary copies and variant recensions of the War Scroll from Cave 4, showing the text had a living textual tradition. Some fragments contain material not in 1QM, including a remarkable self-glorification hymn ("I am counted with the angels...") that suggests an even more developed angelology.
- **1QS (Community Rule) cols. 3–4**: The Two Spirits dualism — Sons of Light vs. Sons of Darkness — is the theological foundation of the War Scroll. The combat described in the War Scroll is the historical/eschatological outworking of the cosmic dualism laid out in 1QS.
- **Songs of the Sabbath Sacrifice (4QShirShabb)**: The angelic liturgy described in these texts provides background for the War Scroll's picture of angels present in the war camp. The Yahad's worship was understood to participate in the angelic worship of the heavenly Temple.
- **Pesher Nahum; Pesher Habakkuk**: The identification of the Kittim as Rome in these commentary texts confirms the War Scroll's use of the same designation.

**Other Ancient Texts**
- **1 Maccabees and 2 Maccabees**: The historical Maccabean battles — especially the battle of Emmaus (1 Macc. 4), where a small force defeated a superior enemy — provide the typological pattern the War Scroll expects to repeat on a cosmic scale.
- **Josephus, *Jewish War***: Josephus's account of the Essenes bearing arms and enduring torture during the revolt (JW 2.152–153) may reflect the War Scroll tradition that some members were expected to fight in the final war.
- **Roman military manuals (Vegetius, *Epitoma Rei Militaris*)**: Several formations described in the War Scroll correspond to Roman military practice, suggesting the author had direct knowledge of Roman tactics — either through observation or captured military documents.
- **The Sibylline Oracles**: The expectation of a great final war followed by cosmic renewal is shared across a range of Second Temple Jewish texts, reflecting a widespread apocalyptic atmosphere rather than a uniquely Qumranic invention.

---

## What a Modern Reader Might Miss

**1. "Kittim" is a living code word, not a historical reference.**
The War Scroll's enemies include "the Kittim of Assyria" and "the Kittim of Egypt" — language drawn from Numbers 24:24 and Daniel 11:30. But for the Qumran community writing in the first century BCE, the Kittim designated Rome — specifically the Roman legions advancing through Judea and Egypt under Pompey and his successors. This is confirmed by the scroll's description of Kittim officers and their battle tactics, which correspond to Roman rather than Greek or Assyrian practice. The Kittim designation allowed the text to connect Rome to prophetic denunciation of ancient enemies while keeping the contemporary reference available to insiders. This kind of coded reference to contemporary powers was standard apocalyptic technique; the same move is made in Revelation's "Babylon" for Rome (Rev. 17–18).

**2. The purity regulations are not squeamishness — they are pneumatology.**
The requirement that combatants be ritually pure, sexually abstinent during the war period, and free from physical defects seems bizarre to modern readers. But the logic is precise: the holy angels are physically present in the war camp (col. 7 explicitly states "for the holy angels are together with their armies"). The regulations that govern the Temple — where the divine presence dwells — govern the war camp for the same reason. The war camp is a mobile Holy of Holies. A sexually active soldier would be as disqualifying as a priest with a skin disease officiating at the altar. The war is not only military; it is liturgical.

**3. The three-round battle structure is theological, not tactical.**
The pattern in which the Sons of Darkness win the first engagement, the Sons of Light recover and win the second, and victory is finally secured in the third round is not a realistic battle plan — it is a theological narrative about how God's salvation operates. The pattern echoes the Psalms' recurring structure of lament (enemy seems to have won) / confidence (God will act) / praise (God has acted). The community is being taught through the battle narrative that apparent defeat before the final victory is not evidence that God has failed; it is the expected pattern. This is directly relevant to their experience of continued Roman domination.

**4. Michael's role is a major development in angelology.**
The naming of Michael as the angelic commander of the Sons of Light (col. 17) is a significant moment in the development of Jewish angelology. In Daniel 10:13, Michael is "one of the chief princes" and "the great prince who stands for the sons of your people" (Dan. 12:1). The War Scroll promotes him to commanding general of the heavenly army in explicit terms. This Michael tradition feeds directly into Revelation 12:7 ("Michael and his angels fighting against the dragon"). The War Scroll is a crucial link in the chain between Daniel's Michael and the New Testament's.

**5. The scroll is also a failure document.**
The community that wrote the War Scroll and preserved it in Cave 1 did not fight the final eschatological war. They were destroyed by the Romans in 68 CE — by the very Kittim they expected God to vanquish. The scrolls were hidden, the settlement burned, the community ended. The War Scroll is therefore not just a text about anticipated victory; it is evidence of a hope that was not fulfilled in the way its authors expected. This makes it more, not less, interesting as a theological document: it raises sharp questions about prophetic interpretation, about the relationship between historical expectation and symbolic meaning, and about what happens when communities built on eschatological certainty face historical annihilation.

**6. The scroll assumes corporate identity that modern Western readers lack.**
The War Scroll makes no sense if individuals fight for personal survival or personal glory. Every instruction assumes that individual soldiers are interchangeable representatives of a collective — Israel, the Sons of Light, the lot of God. A soldier's death is not a tragedy in the modern sense; it is a contribution to the corporate victory. The war is fought by the community as a single organism. This corporate solidarity is rooted in the community's covenant identity: they are Israel, not merely a group of Israelites, and Israel's victory is decreed regardless of individual survival. This is a radically different anthropology from modern Western individualism.

---

## Why This Text Isn't in Your Bible

The War Scroll was never a candidate for any biblical canon. Its genre — a detailed battle plan for an eschatological war — places it in the category of practical instruction for a specific community's anticipated future, not prophetic writing claiming to be the word of God in the traditional sense.

More tellingly, the war it describes never happened — at least not in any form the scroll's authors would have recognized. The Qumran community was destroyed by the Kittim (Rome) before the eschatological war could begin. The scroll's confident prediction of Israel's forty-year victory over Rome was simply wrong on its own terms, at least in its expected historical timeline. A text whose central subject — the final eschatological war leading to Israel's military triumph over Rome — had manifestly not occurred could not be received as authoritative Scripture.

The War Scroll also belonged to a sectarian tradition that died with the Qumran community. The rabbinic Judaism that survived 70 CE moved emphatically away from apocalyptic military eschatology — the catastrophic failure of the two revolts against Rome (66–70 CE and 132–135 CE) made such speculation dangerous and practically futile. The rabbis redirected eschatological hope toward Torah study and legal observance, not military preparation. Christianity, which did inherit significant apocalyptic traditions, received them through channels that had already transformed the War Scroll's literal military imagery into spiritual categories — the armor of God, the war against spiritual principalities and powers, the Lamb defeating the Beast not through military conquest but through death and resurrection.

---

## Timeline

| Date | Event |
|---|---|
| **586 BCE** | Babylon destroys Jerusalem; beginning of the long era of Gentile domination of Israel that the War Scroll expects to end |
| **168–164 BCE** | Antiochus IV desecrates the Temple; Maccabean revolt; typological precedent for the final war |
| **c. 150 BCE** | Qumran community founded; separation from Jerusalem begins |
| **c. 100–50 BCE** | War Scroll composed in its present form; 1QM manuscript copied c. 50–25 BCE |
| **63 BCE** | Pompey captures Jerusalem; Rome becomes the Kittim of the War Scroll |
| **37 BCE** | Herod the Great takes the throne with Roman support; Roman domination of Judea intensified |
| **6 CE** | Judea becomes a Roman province; tension intensifies |
| **66 CE** | First Jewish Revolt against Rome begins |
| **68 CE (approx.)** | Roman Legio X Fretensis advances toward Qumran; community hides scrolls in caves |
| **68 CE** | Qumran settlement destroyed; the anticipated war between the Sons of Light and the Kittim ends in the defeat of the Sons of Light |
| **70 CE** | Jerusalem falls; Temple destroyed |
| **1946/1947 CE** | Cave 1 discovered; 1QM among the first major scrolls recovered |
| **1955 CE** | Yigael Yadin publishes the first major scholarly edition of the War Scroll |
| **1977 CE** | Yadin publishes a revised critical edition; War Scroll scholarship enters its mature phase |

---

*HESED notes: The War Scroll is the most uncomfortable major DSS text for both Jewish and Christian readers, because it demands engagement with a tradition of violent, divinely-mandated warfare that neither tradition has found easy to appropriate. Do not resolve this discomfort too quickly. Note that the scroll's violence is always in the service of cosmic justice — the defeat of the forces that have oppressed the righteous — and that the human soldiers are consistently subordinated to divine agency: God wins the war, not the Sons of Light. The closest New Testament parallel is not the Crusade tradition (which the scroll does not support) but the Apocalypse of John, where the Lamb defeats the Beast not by military prowess but by the decree of God made certain before the foundation of the world. The War Scroll's most enduring contribution may be its insistence that history has a direction, that evil does not have the last word, and that the community of the righteous lives between promise and fulfillment — a theology of hope that the New Testament inherits and transforms but does not invent.*
